transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well… thank you for seeing me. I’m not sure if I’m explaining it right, but I came because since my grandson was killed, something in me feels… shut off. My daughter can sit right next to me and hold my hand, and I know I love her, of course I do, but I can’t feel the warmth of it inside me. It’s like the feeling won’t come through.
Since your grandson passed away, have you noticed that you no longer take pleasure in things you used to enjoy, or that you’ve lost interest in activities or people that were important to you?

Yes… I think so. I don’t mean to sound ungrateful, because my daughter has been so kind to me. She’ll sit right beside me and hold my hand, and I know in my head that I love her. I do. But since my grandson was killed, I just… I can’t feel the warmth of it inside me. It’s like it doesn’t reach me, if that makes sense.
Have you been feeling guilty or blaming yourself for things since your grandson passed away?

I… I don’t know that I’d say I blame myself, exactly. I keep wondering if there was something I should have done, but I’m not sure that’s the same thing. I don’t want to make it sound worse than it is. Is that… is that what you mean by guilt?
Have you noticed that you feel emotionally numb or that you’re not able to experience joy, sadness, or other feelings the way you used to?

Yes… I think that is exactly it, though I don’t want to overstate it. Since my grandson was killed, it’s like something in me just went quiet. My daughter can sit right beside me and hold my hand, and I know I love her—I know that—but I can’t feel the warmth of it inside me at all. It’s a terrible thing to say, isn’t it? But that’s how it feels.
Since your grandson passed away, have you felt down or in a low mood most of the day, nearly every day?

I’m not sure I’d call it that, doctor. I mean… I have been sad, of course, but “most of the day nearly every day” sounds so definite. I don’t know if I can answer that properly. Some days I just feel quiet and heavy, but I wouldn’t want to say the wrong thing.
Can you tell me if, since your grandson passed away, you’ve felt down or in a low mood on most days, even if it's not all day long?

I… I’m sorry, I don’t know how to answer that cleanly. Some days I do feel very low, yes, but when you say “most days,” I start second-guessing myself. I don’t want to say yes if that makes it sound stronger than it is. It’s been heavy, but I’m not sure I’ve been keeping track properly.
Can you tell me if, since your grandson passed away, you’ve felt down or in a low mood on most days, even if it's not all day long?

I’m sorry, doctor, I still don’t think I can say for certain. It has felt very heavy at times, and I know I haven’t been myself… but “most days” is hard for me to judge. I don’t want to give you the wrong answer just to be agreeable.
Since your grandson passed away, have you noticed that you no longer take pleasure in things you used to enjoy, or that you’ve lost interest in activities or people that were important to you?

I suppose… yes, in a way. I don’t want to sound ungrateful, because my daughter has been so kind to me. She’ll sit right beside me and hold my hand, and I know I love her—I do know that—but since my grandson was killed, I can’t seem to feel the warmth of it inside me. It’s like I understand it, but I don’t feel it the way I should. Does that make sense?
Doctor: Have you found yourself feeling down or in a low mood even on days when you aren’t directly reminded of your grandson’s passing?

I’m not sure I can separate it that neatly, doctor. I mean… even when nothing obvious has reminded me, I may still feel a bit low, but I don’t know if it’s really “for no reason” or if it’s all just underneath everything. I don’t want to overstate it.
Have you found that you no longer care to spend time with people you used to enjoy being around, or that activities you used to like don’t interest you anymore?

I don’t want to make it sound as if I don’t care about people, because I do. My daughter especially has been so good to me. But… yes, something feels shut off. She can sit right next to me and hold my hand, and I know I love her, but I can’t feel the warmth of it inside the way I used to. I came in because of that, really. Since my grandson was killed, it’s like the feeling just won’t come through. Does that answer what you mean?
Can you tell me if there have been days when you felt down or in a low mood even when nothing happened to specifically remind you of your grandson's passing?

I’m not really sure, doctor. I don’t think I can say clearly that there are days like that when it has nothing to do with him. It all feels sort of… mixed together underneath, if that makes sense. I don’t want to give you the wrong answer.
Can you tell me if there have been times when you felt down or in a low mood even when you weren’t thinking about your grandson or anything related to his passing?

I’m sorry, I still don’t think I can separate it that well. I might not be actively thinking about him every minute, but it feels like it’s still there in the background. So I wouldn’t want to say yes, exactly, because I’m not sure that would be accurate. Does that make sense?

Can you tell me if you’ve noticed a change in how you feel about activities you used to enjoy—like whether they still bring you pleasure or satisfaction, even when you’re not reminded of your grandson?

Yes… I think so. I don’t want to overstate it, but things that should feel comforting or nice just don’t quite reach me now. Like I said, my daughter can be right there beside me, holding my hand, and I know I love her—of course I do—but I can’t feel that warmth inside me the way I should. It feels awful to say that. Is that the sort of thing you’re asking?
Can you tell me if there have been times when you felt down or in a low mood even when you weren’t thinking about your grandson or anything related to his passing?

I think I understand what you’re asking, but… I’m still not sure I can really separate it like that. Even if I’m not directly thinking about him, it feels like it’s sort of sitting there underneath everything. So I don’t want to say yes if that isn’t quite right. Maybe I just haven’t noticed a time when it felt completely unrelated. Is that okay to say?
Can you tell me if there have been times when you didn’t take pleasure in things you used to enjoy, even when you weren’t reminded of your grandson or thinking about his passing?

Yes… I think that has happened. I don’t mean to sound dramatic, but since my grandson was killed, even the things that ought to feel good don’t seem to come through.

Like, my daughter can be sitting right beside me, holding my hand, and I know I love her, I do… but I can’t feel the warmth of it inside the way I should. It makes me feel ashamed to say that, because she’s trying so hard. But that’s what I mean, I suppose. Is that answering it the right way?
